data.body:
## EMPIRICAL VALIDATION of recommendation part 1 — the anti-vacuity assertion caught a new vacuous guard AS IT WAS BEING WRITTEN

Recording this because it is the strongest evidence in this epic, and it was produced by accident
rather than by looking for it.

Bug 9baf-06ce-60ba-4f0b (two CloudWatch alarms with no `alarm_actions`) was dispatched with a
requirement drawn from this epic's recommendation: add a guard, AND give the guard an
anti-vacuity assertion that its scanned population is non-empty.

What happened, in the agent's own account:

> The anti-vacuity assertion earned its place within a minute of existing. My first parser
> matched the resource header against the *masked* text, where quoted strings are blanked, so it
> found **zero** blocks — and `test_every_alarm_declares_alarm_actions` **passed vacuously**
> while the `>= 13` assertion failed loudly and exposed the bug.

So a BRAND NEW guard, written by an agent that had been explicitly warned about vacuity, in a
session whose entire theme was vacuous checks, was itself vacuous on first attempt. The only
reason it did not ship that way is the population assertion.

## Why this matters for the recommendation

It answers the strongest objection to part 1 — that an anti-vacuity convention is bureaucratic
overhead for a rare failure. The measured rate here is not rare. Across this session:

- 5 pre-existing guards found vacuous (34c2 plus 8a5e's four)
- 11 CI gate steps unguarded (1909)
- 1 test double more permissive than the real tool (c5b3)
- 2 tests skip-masked into permanent non-execution (a371)
- **1 new guard vacuous on first write, caught by the assertion (9baf)**

The last is qualitatively different from the others. The rest are archaeology — debt accumulated
before anyone was watching. This one is a NEW defect, introduced by an informed author, and
prevented. That is the difference between the closed prior-art tickets (6924, 4168, 003d — all
remedial sweeps) and a mechanism.

It also cost essentially nothing: one assertion, written at the same time as the guard, by the
same author, in the same file.

## Refinement to part 1 this suggests

The 9baf guard's failure mode is worth generalizing: the parser found zero blocks because it
searched TEXT THAT HAD BEEN DELIBERATELY BLANKED (comment/string masking). That is a plausible
mistake for any scanning check, not a one-off. So the convention should be stated as a property
of the POPULATION, not of the parse:

    assert the scanned population is non-empty AND matches an independently-known count

9baf used `>= 13` — a number the author knew from outside the parser. A bare `len(x) > 0` would
also have caught this instance, but an independently-sourced expected count is strictly stronger
and no harder to write.

## Also worth noting for part 3 (mutation proof as expectation)

The same agent mutation-checked both directions: re-deleting the alarm's `alarm_actions` returned
the guard to RED, and pointing the parser at an empty directory failed the COUNT assertion rather
than passing. The second half of that is the anti-vacuity property tested as a first-class
behavior, not assumed.
